La Peste: The city of Oran is struck by an outbreak of plague.
1984: Winston Smith lives under the constant watch of Big Brother.
Sapiens : une brève histoire de l’humani: A history of the human species, from prehistory to the present day.
Devenir: The memoir of the former First Lady of the United States.
Harry Potter et la Chambre des secrets: In his second year at Hogwarts, Harry hears voices in the walls, and pupils are found petrified. The legendary Chamber of Secrets seems to have been opened again.
Le Petit Livre des couleurs: Why did blue become Europeans’ favourite colour? Why is red the colour of both love and anger? In a conversation, the historian Michel Pastoureau tells the history and symbolism of six colours.
Géo Ado: The magazine that shows the world to 10-to-15-year-olds: reports, big photographs, countries and cultures, nature and animals.
Contes de Grimm: Hansel and Gretel, Snow White, Rapunzel, The Town Musicians of Bremen: a selection of the tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.
Notre-Dame du Nil: In Rwanda in the early 1970s, the Notre-Dame du Nil boarding school, high in the hills, takes in the daughters of the elite. Behind the lessons and the prayers, tensions between Hutu and Tutsi pupils foreshadow the violence to come. Prix Renaudot 2012.
Le Gène égoïste: Richard Dawkins invites us to look at evolution from the genes’ point of view: living beings would be “machines” built to pass them on.
Science & Vie Junior: A monthly popular-science magazine for 10-to-15-year-olds: in-depth features, experiments, and news from science and technology.
Rhinocéros: In a small town, the inhabitants turn into rhinoceroses one by one. Bérenger, an ordinary clerk who drinks a little too much, is soon the only one left resisting.
Les Misérables:
Freed from the galleys after nineteen years for stealing a loaf of bread, Jean Valjean is transformed by the kindness of Bishop Myriel. Now a respected man under another name, he takes in Cosette, a child exploited by the Thénardiers, while being relentlessly hunted by Inspector Javert.

From the Battle of Waterloo to the Paris barricades of 1832, Victor Hugo weaves the history of France into the lives of the poorest, and asks a question that runs through the whole novel: can a man change, and will society let him?
Les Fleurs du mal: The collection that caused a scandal when it appeared: Baudelaire sets Spleen against the Ideal, sings of Paris, love, boredom and death, and seeks beauty even in evil.
Vingt mille lieues sous les mers: Sent to hunt down a sea monster, Professor Aronnax, his servant Conseil and the harpooner Ned Land find themselves prisoners aboard the Nautilus, the submarine of the mysterious Captain Nemo. With him, they explore the depths of every sea on the globe.
Max et les Maximonstres: Punished and sent to bed without supper, Max watches his bedroom turn into a forest. He sails away to the land of the Wild Things, who make him their king.
Madame Bovary: Raised on sentimental novels, Emma marries Charles Bovary, a dull country doctor. The boredom of provincial life drives her towards lovers and debts that will be her undoing.
Cyrano de Bergerac: Cyrano, a Gascon cadet, poet and swordsman, secretly loves his cousin Roxane. Convinced that his enormous nose makes him unworthy of her, he lends his words to the handsome Christian, who is courting her.
L’Enfant noir:
Camara Laye tells of his childhood in Kouroussa, in Upper Guinea: his father’s forge and the little black snake that protects him, harvest time at his grandmother’s in Tindican, Koranic school and then French school, and the initiation rites that make him a man.

As the boy continues his studies, first in Conakry and then in Paris, he drifts away from his parents’ world. The book is both a tender tribute to his mother and to a culture, and the story of a wrenching departure: growing up also means leaving.
L’Avare: Harpagon thinks of nothing but his casket full of gold. He wants to marry young Mariane, whom his son Cléante also loves, and to marry his daughter off to a rich old man who would take her “without a dowry”.
L’Origine des espèces: The work in which Darwin sets out the theory of evolution by natural selection: species are not fixed, they change over the generations, and those that survive are the best suited to their environment.
No et moi: Lou, thirteen and two years ahead at school, chooses homelessness as the subject of her class presentation. At the Gare d’Austerlitz she meets No, an eighteen-year-old girl living on the street, and decides to help her whatever it takes.
L’Afrique noire est mal partie: In the wake of independence, the agronomist René Dumont takes a critical look at the economic choices of the new African states and argues for putting peasant farming first.
La Bar-Mitsva: In 1930s Algiers, a rabbi’s cat eats the household parrot and starts to talk. He wants to have his bar mitzvah and debates God with his master, much to the rabbi’s dismay.
Devine combien je t’aime: Before going to sleep, Little Nutbrown Hare wants to show Big Nutbrown Hare how much he loves him: as wide as his arms, as high as he can hop, as far as the river. But Big Nutbrown Hare loves him even more.
Une brève histoire du temps: Where does the universe come from? Did it have a beginning, and will it have an end? Stephen Hawking explains space, time, the Big Bang and black holes without equations.
La Terre vue du ciel: Aerial photographs taken all over the world, each with a text explaining what it reveals about our planet and the people who live on it.
Le Garçon en pyjama rayé: Nine-year-old Bruno leaves Berlin to follow his father, who has been made commandant of a camp. On the other side of the barbed wire, he befriends Shmuel, a boy who always wears striped pyjamas. A story told at a child’s height, by a boy who does not understand what the reader does.
Le Comte de Monte-Cristo: On the day of his engagement, the young sailor Edmond Dantès is arrested on a false denunciation and locked up in the Château d’If. Fourteen years later he escapes, rich with the treasure revealed to him by the Abbé Faria, and returns as the Count of Monte Cristo to take revenge, one by one, on those who betrayed him.
Tintin au Tibet: Tintin learns that his friend Chang’s plane has crashed in the Himalayas. Convinced that he is alive, he sets out to find him with Captain Haddock, despite the mountains, the cold and the rumours of a yeti.
Le Hobbit: Bilbo Baggins, a home-loving hobbit, is swept along by the wizard Gandalf and thirteen dwarves on a quest to the Lonely Mountain, where the dragon Smaug guards a stolen treasure. On the way, he finds a ring that makes him invisible.
Contes: Little Red Riding Hood, Cinderella, Bluebeard, Puss in Boots, Hop-o’-My-Thumb, Sleeping Beauty: Perrault’s tales, each followed by its moral in verse.
Elmer: Elmer is a patchwork elephant of every colour. Tired of being different, he rolls in grey berries to look like the others.
Homo Deus: Having largely overcome famine, plague and war, what will humanity seek next? Yuval Noah Harari imagines a future in which algorithms and biotechnology change what it means to be human.
La Diligence: Lucky Luke escorts a Wells Fargo stagecoach carrying gold across the West, with a set of passengers as colourful as they are suspicious.
Les Cahiers d’Esther: Esther is ten and tells us about her life: school, her friends, her big brother, screens, boys. Every page comes from what a real little girl told the author.
La Chenille qui fait des trous: A very hungry little caterpillar eats one apple on Monday, two pears on Tuesday… and grows and grows until it turns into a butterfly.
Naruto: Naruto Uzumaki, an unruly apprentice ninja shunned by his village, dreams of becoming Hokage, the most powerful ninja of all, so that people will finally recognise him.
À l’aube d’une grande aventure: Luffy has eaten a Devil Fruit that made his body as stretchy as rubber. He sets sail to gather a crew, find the legendary treasure One Piece and become King of the Pirates.
J’aime lire: Every month, an illustrated novel, comics and games for 7-to-10-year-olds learning to read on their own.
Paroles: Poems in everyday language: Barbara, The Dunce, To Paint the Portrait of a Bird, Breakfast. Prévert mixes tenderness, humour and revolt.
Mortelle Adèle: Adèle doesn’t like her parents, her cat Ajax or other children. One-page gags, fierce and very funny.
Eragon: Eragon, a young farm boy, finds a blue stone in the mountains that turns out to be a dragon’s egg. When the dragon Saphira hatches, he becomes a Dragon Rider, and the target of King Galbatorix.
Vendredi ou la Vie sauvage: Shipwrecked on a desert island, Robinson tries to rebuild the society he left behind: he farms, builds and makes laws. The arrival of Friday upsets this order and teaches him another way of living.
Le Vieux qui lisait des romans d’amour: In El Idilio, a remote village in the Ecuadorian Amazon, Antonio José Bolívar knows the forest better than anyone. When a female jaguar starts killing men, he is the one sent to track her down. A short novel about nature, old age and the love of reading.
Cahier d’un retour au pays natal:
A long prose poem written as Césaire was leaving Paris for Martinique. He cries out the poverty of his island and the legacy of slavery, and for the first time forcefully claims “négritude”.

A founding text of twentieth-century French-language poetry, hailed by André Breton as “the greatest lyrical monument of our time”.
Printemps silencieux: The biologist Rachel Carson shows how pesticides such as DDT poison soil, rivers and birds. This book founded the modern environmental movement.
Phosphore: The magazine for secondary-school students: careers and further study, news, society and culture. Useful for preparing university applications and the oral exam.
Fables: The Crow and the Fox, The Grasshopper and the Ant, The Wolf and the Lamb… La Fontaine’s best-known fables, in which animals speak to show up human failings.
Une histoire de la lecture: From clay tablets to paperbacks, from reading aloud to silent reading, Alberto Manguel tells how people have read through the centuries, and what reading has made of them.
Germinal: Étienne Lantier, an unemployed worker, is taken on at the Voreux mine in northern France. He discovers the miners’ poverty and leads a strike that ends in tragedy.
Aya de Yopougon: Abidjan, late 1970s. Nineteen-year-old Aya wants to become a doctor, while her friends Adjoua and Bintou prefer nightspots and boys. A funny, tender chronicle of the working-class district of Yopougon.
L’Aventure ambiguë:
Samba Diallo, a son of the Diallobé aristocracy, first receives the strict teaching of the Koranic master. His family then decides to send him to the white man’s school, and later to Paris to study philosophy.

Caught between two cultures, two ways of thinking about God and the world, the young man gradually loses his bearings. This philosophical novel asks what one gains and what one loses in “learning to bind wood to wood”.
Astérix le Gaulois: The year is 50 BC. All of Gaul is occupied by the Romans… All? No! One village of indomitable Gauls still holds out, thanks to the magic potion of the druid Getafix. The centurion Crismus Bonus wants to discover its secret.
Le Grand Meaulnes: Augustin Meaulnes, a new boarder at the school in Sainte-Agathe, loses his way one evening and stumbles on a mysterious estate where a strange celebration is taking place. There he glimpses Yvonne de Galais, and spends years searching for the way back. The narrator, François, tells of this quest for a lost paradise.
Le Crime de l’Orient-Express: Stopped by snow in the middle of Yugoslavia, the Orient Express comes to a halt. In the morning, a passenger is found stabbed in his compartment. Hercule Poirot investigates among twelve travellers who all have an alibi.
Le Cid: Rodrigue loves Chimène, and Chimène loves him. But to avenge his father’s honour, Rodrigue must kill the father of the woman he loves in a duel. Torn between love and duty, each of them must choose.
Discours sur le colonialisme: A short, fierce pamphlet in which Aimé Césaire takes apart colonial discourse and shows that colonisation dehumanises the colonised as much as the coloniser.
Le Lion, la Sorcière blanche et l’Armoir: Sent to the countryside during the war, Peter, Susan, Edmund and Lucy discover, at the back of a wardrobe, the kingdom of Narnia, held in endless winter by the White Witch.
Les Contes d’Amadou Koumba: Birago Diop writes down the tales told to him by the griot Amadou Koumba: Leuk the Hare, Bouki the Hyena and many others scheme, blunder and learn. A way into the oral tradition of West Africa.
Les Contes du chat perché: On a farm, Delphine and Marinette talk with the animals, who help them escape their parents’ anger. The wolf, the stag, the peacock and the oxen share adventures full of mischief with them.
Bel-Ami: Georges Duroy, a penniless former non-commissioned officer, drifts into journalism almost by chance. Charming and unscrupulous, he uses women to climb the ladder of Parisian society.
L’homme qui prenait sa femme pour un cha: The neurologist Oliver Sacks tells the stories of patients with astonishing disorders: a man who can no longer recognise faces, a woman who can no longer feel her body. Deeply human accounts that show how the brain builds our world.
Une si longue lettre: Just after her husband’s death, Ramatoulaye writes to her friend Aïssatou. She looks back on her marriage, on the betrayal of Modou, who took a second wife, and on her choice to stay when Aïssatou chose to leave. A short, powerful novel in letters about the place of women in modern Senegal.
Kirikou et la sorcière: Kirikou, tiny but quick, is born in a West African village that the sorceress Karaba has robbed of its water and its men. He is determined to find out why she is so wicked.
Bon appétit ! Monsieur Lapin: Mr Rabbit no longer likes carrots. He goes to see what the frog, the bird, the fish and the whale eat… and finally the fox, who likes rabbits.
Ceux qui restent: Pierrot, Mimile and Antoine, childhood friends now in their seventies, meet again at the funeral of Antoine’s wife. A secret uncovered that day sends the three grumpy old men off on the road.
Les Trois Brigands: Three fearsome robbers, armed with a blunderbuss, a pepper-blower and a huge red axe, hold up stagecoaches. One night the only passenger they find is a little orphan, Tiffany, who asks them what they do with all their gold.
Le Loup qui voulait changer de couleur: Wolf finds black gloomy. Every day of the week he tries a new colour, but is never satisfied.
Gruffalo: A little mouse takes a walk in the woods. To scare off the fox, the owl and the snake who want to eat her, she invents a terrible monster, the Gruffalo. But what happens when the Gruffalo turns out to be real?
Roméo et Juliette: In Verona, the Montagues and the Capulets hate each other. Romeo and Juliet, children of the two families, fall in love and marry in secret.
Les Fourberies de Scapin: While their fathers are away, Octave and Léandre have pledged themselves to young women without fortune. The valet Scapin, a master of tricks, sets out to fool the two old men and get the lovers out of trouble.
Un long chemin vers la liberté:
Nelson Mandela’s autobiography: his childhood in the Transkei, his studies, his fight against apartheid with the ANC, the Rivonia trial and twenty-seven years in prison, eighteen of them on Robben Island.

The book ends with his release in 1990 and his election as President of South Africa in 1994. A testimony to patience, resistance and reconciliation.
Le Tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours: Phileas Fogg bets twenty thousand pounds that he can travel around the world in eighty days. With his valet Passepartout, and pursued by Inspector Fix, he sets off in a race against the clock.
Le Chien des Baskerville: A family legend tells of a monstrous hound that haunts the Devon moors and pursues the heirs of the Baskervilles. After the suspicious death of Sir Charles, Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson are called in to protect his nephew.
Indignez-vous !: A former Resistance fighter and one of the drafters of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Stéphane Hessel, aged 93, calls on young people not to stay indifferent.
Oscar et la dame rose: Ten-year-old Oscar is in hospital and knows he is going to die. Granny Rose, a volunteer visitor, suggests he live each day as if it were ten years, and write to God.
Okapi: A twice-monthly magazine for 10-to-15-year-olds: the news explained, school life, science, culture and comics.
Wonder: Auggie was born with a facial difference and has always been home-schooled. At ten, he starts middle school. The novel lets Auggie, his sister and his classmates speak in turn: a year of stares, cruelty and unexpected friendships.
Éthiopiques: A collection by Senghor, poet and future president of Senegal. His poems, written to be spoken to the kora or the balafon, celebrate Africa, its women and its landscapes, and seek to reconcile two cultures.
Bébés chouettes: One night, Sarah, Percy and Bill wake up: their owl mother is gone. Huddled together on their branch, they wait for her.
Images Doc: A richly illustrated nonfiction magazine for 8-to-12-year-olds: history, animals, science and countries of the world, with infographics and a comic strip.
La Tragédie du roi Christophe: After Haiti’s independence, the former slave Henri Christophe has himself crowned king. To make his people a nation, he imposes forced labour and builds a vast citadel. Aimé Césaire shows how the dream of liberation can turn into tyranny.
Fahrenheit 451: Montag is a fireman: his job is not to put out fires but to burn books, which the state has banned. An encounter leads him to read one, and then to question everything.
Le Racisme expliqué à ma fille: In the form of a dialogue with his ten-year-old daughter, Tahar Ben Jelloun explains what racism is, where it comes from and how it can be fought.
Astérix et Cléopâtre: Cleopatra has bet Caesar that the Egyptians will build him a palace in three months. The architect Edifis calls on Getafix for help, who sets off for Alexandria with Asterix, Obelix and Dogmatix.
Ils étaient dix: Ten strangers are invited to an island off the Devon coast by a host who never appears. On the first evening, a voice accuses each of them of a crime that went unpunished. Then, one by one, they die, just as in the nursery rhyme hanging in their rooms.
C’est moi le plus fort: The wolf has eaten well and goes for a walk to check that everyone agrees he is the strongest: Little Red Riding Hood, the three little pigs, the seven dwarfs… until he meets someone who shuts him up for good.
Persepolis:
In black and white, Marjane Satrapi tells of her childhood in Tehran, from the fall of the Shah to the Islamic Revolution and the war with Iraq. A little girl who wants to be a prophet discovers politics, repression and her family’s courage.

The story mixes history and daily life: the compulsory veil at school, forbidden music cassettes, imprisoned uncles. A graphic novel that has become a classic, studied in middle and secondary school alike.
Cosmos: Based on the famous television series, a journey through the universe and the history of science, from the astronomers of Antiquity to the Voyager probes.
Le Petit Prince:
A pilot stranded in the Sahara Desert meets a little boy from another planet. The little prince tells him about his asteroid, his rose, and the strange grown-ups he met along the way: a king, a conceited man, a businessman, a geographer.

From the fox, he learns what it means to “tame”. A poetic tale, illustrated by the author, that can be read at any age and tells us that “what is essential is invisible to the eye”.
On a marché sur la Lune: Professor Calculus’s rocket finally takes off, with Tintin, Snowy, Captain Haddock… and two unexpected stowaways on board. Fifteen years before Apollo 11, Hergé imagines the first human steps on the Moon.
Les Fiancés de l’hiver: Clumsy, quiet Ophelia can read the past of objects and travel through mirrors. She is betrothed to Thorn, a cold man from the Dragon clan, and must leave her ark of Anima for the Citaceleste, a floating city full of intrigue and illusion.
Le Jeu de l’amour et du hasard: To observe the suitor chosen for her, Silvia trades places with her maid. She does not know that Dorante has had the same idea with his valet.
L’Œil du loup: In a zoo, a boy from Africa stands every day in front of the enclosure of a one-eyed wolf. Little by little, the boy’s eye and the wolf’s eye tell each other their stories: the Far North, the hunt, yellow, grey and green Africa.
Allah n’est pas obligé: Birahima, about ten years old, sets off to find his aunt in Liberia and becomes a child soldier. He tells of the war with cheeky bravado, using four dictionaries to explain his words. Prix Renaudot 2000.
Petit-Bleu et Petit-Jaune: Little Blue and Little Yellow are the best of friends. One day they hug each other so hard that they turn green, and their parents no longer recognise them.
L’Arabe du futur: The son of a Syrian father and a Breton mother, little Riad grows up in Gaddafi’s Libya and then in a Syrian village. Through a child’s eyes, he tells of his father’s pan-Arab dreams and the reality he discovers.
Harry Potter à l’école des sorciers:
On his eleventh birthday, Harry Potter, an orphan mistreated by his aunt and uncle, learns that he is a wizard and that a place awaits him at Hogwarts. There he discovers Quidditch, makes two friends, Ron and Hermione, and slowly learns what happened to his parents.

Behind the magic and the humour, a novel about friendship, courage and choosing who you want to be.
Petit Pays:
Gabriel is ten and lives in Bujumbura, in the Kinanira district, with his French father, his Rwandan mother and his little sister Ana. With his friends from the cul-de-sac, he spends his days stealing mangoes, building boats and setting the world to rights in an old Volkswagen van.

Then, in 1993, everything changes: his parents separate, the president is assassinated, civil war breaks out in Burundi and the genocide of the Tutsi begins in neighbouring Rwanda. Gaël Faye tells of the end of a childhood and violence bursting into a world that seemed peaceful. Prix Goncourt des lycéens 2016.
Le Malade imaginaire: Argan believes he is ill and wants to marry his daughter Angélique to a doctor, so as to have one in the house. The maid Toinette and his brother Béralde will do everything to open his eyes. Molière’s last comedy: he died shortly after one of its performances.
Antigone:
Defying King Creon’s ban, Antigone wants to bury her brother Polynices. Jean Anouilh retells the Greek myth during the German Occupation and turns it into a clash between two logics: the one that says no, and the one that governs.

First staged in Paris in 1944, the play is one of the most studied in the last year of middle school, for its direct language and the question it leaves open: who is right, Antigone or Creon?
Le Journal d’Anne Frank:
From June 1942 to August 1944, Anne Frank, a young German Jewish girl, lives in hiding with her family and four other people in the “Secret Annex”, a concealed apartment in Amsterdam. In her diary, which she calls Kitty, she writes about fear, the lack of privacy and the quarrels, but also about her reading, her first feelings and her dreams of becoming a writer.

Arrested with her family in August 1944, she died in Bergen-Belsen a few months later. Her father, the only survivor, had the diary published in 1947: it has become one of the most widely read testimonies in the world.
Hunger Games:
Every year, the Capitol forces the twelve districts of Panem to send two teenagers to fight to the death in a televised arena. To save her little sister, Katniss Everdeen volunteers.

In the arena she must survive, but also perform for the cameras and the sponsors without losing what makes her human. An action novel that is also about propaganda, spectacle and revolt.
